patient.chief_complaint: Visual zigzag followed by severe headache — now with 2-3 episodes per month
patient.hpi:
A 35-year-old Black woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic with a 7-year history of recurrent visual aura followed by severe headaches that have increased in frequency over the past 6 months from 1-2 to 2-3 per month. Each episode begins with a small bright spot in her central vision that gradually expands into a multicolored zigzag pattern (fortification spectra) spreading outward over 20-30 minutes, leaving a temporary blind area. As the visual aura fades, she develops a severe left-sided throbbing headache (8/10) with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia that lasts 6-10 hours. She often needs to go to a dark room and cannot function during episodes.

She reports that sumatriptan 50 mg (prescribed by her PCP 2 years ago) is effective when taken early in the headache phase but stops working if she delays treatment. She takes it approximately twice per month. She identifies sleep disruption, wine, and intense physical exertion as personal triggers. She is a nurse and has been working double shifts frequently due to understaffing, which correlates with the increased frequency. She is not on hormonal contraception. She had hypertension treated with lifestyle modification (BP 128/78 today) and no other medical history. She denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any episode characteristics that differ from her usual pattern.
pmh: No diabetes, no cardiac disease, no prior neurological diagnosis

family_history: Mother had migraines throughout her 30s and 40s; father had hypertension; no stroke or coagulopathy history

optimal_actions.action: Take a structured headache and aura history against ICHD-3 1.2: number of attacks, aura modality and full reversibility, gradual spread over at least five minutes, duration of each symptom between five and sixty minutes, unilaterality, temporal relation to the headache, and a documented red-flag review. This is the diagnostic test for this condition
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 1.2 criteria documented item by item against the reference set for this subtype, with the red-flag review recorded

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

critical_actions: Address modifiable triggers (sleep deprivation from shift work)
Initiate preventive therapy — propranolol attractive as it treats both stage 1 HTN and migraine [Holland_2012]
contraindicated_actions: Do not start combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception
Do not co-administer triptans with ergotamines
Do not assume new-onset HTN is the cause of migraine attacks without re-examining the diagnostic criteria
key_reasoning_points: Comorbid HTN does not change the migraine diagnosis but informs preventive selection (favour beta-blocker)
Sumatriptan is not contraindicated at stage 1 HTN, but caution and BP monitoring are warranted
Shift-work sleep deprivation is a major modifiable trigger and is plausibly driving the recent frequency increase

red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on hypertensive headache or PRES
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stage 1 HTN is comorbid; it does not by itself cause stereotyped migraine with aura and informs preventive choice rather than the diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Mild HTN + visual symptoms could suggest hypertensive retinopathy or TIA
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stage 1 HTN (128/78) does not cause visual symptoms; 7-year identical history predates HTN; classic migraine aura pattern

clinical_assessment.impression: Structured headache and aura history taken against ICHD-3 1.2. 4 of the four criterion-C characteristics are documented — the diagnosis is met on the history, which is the only test that establishes it. The distinction from a transient ischaemic attack is made here and not by imaging: aura spreads gradually over minutes and is positive before it is negative, whereas ischaemia is abrupt and negative from the outset. Imaging is for the red flags this history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

1. BETA-BLOCKERS (propranolol, metoprolol): First-line for BOTH migraine prevention AND hypertension — ideal dual-indication

4. TOPIRAMATE: Effective for migraine prevention but not antihypertensive; second-line if beta-blocker not tolerated
5. AMITRIPTYLINE: Avoid in hypertensive patients without adequate BP control; safe when BP controlled

output.summary: DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — SUMATRIPTAN IN HYPERTENSION Findings: Sumatriptan is a coronary and cerebral vasoconstrictor (5-HT1B agonist). In Stage 1 HTN (128/78) without cardiac disease, sumatriptan is SAFE at standard doses. Avoid if uncontrolled HTN (>160/100) or known coronary artery disease. PROPRANOLOL + SUMATRIPTAN: Mild interaction — propranolol can increase sumatriptan plasma levels by ~70% due to CYP2D6 inhibition. Monitor for excessive triptan effect; may reduce sumatriptan dose to 25-50 mg when on propranolol. CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 50 mg safe with Stage 1 HTN. Reduce to 25-50 mg when propranolol is initiated. Sumatriptan safe in Stage 1 HTN; propranolol increases sumatriptan levels — reduce dose to 25-50 mg when on propranolol

LITERATURE SEARCH: Migraine in Black Women — Disparities and Management KEY FINDINGS:
1. UNDERDIAGNOSIS: Black women have historically been underdiagnosed with migraine and undertreated; this represents a healthcare disparity
2. CARDIOVASCULAR RISK: Migraine with aura in Black women who also have hypertension represents elevated cardiovascular risk; PRIORITIZE cardiovascular risk factor management
3. STROKE RISK: Migraine with aura is an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke; risk is additive with hypertension and smoking
4. BLOOD PRESSURE CONTROL: Target BP <130/80 in migraineurs with HTN to reduce overall stroke risk
5. TRIPTAN SAFETY: Safe at current BP of 128/78; reassess if BP rises CONCLUSION: Excellent BP control is essential. Propranolol addresses both conditions. Screen for cardiovascular risk factors annually. Migraine with aura + hypertension increases stroke risk; BP target <130/80; propranolol addresses both
